name: Power-assisted liposuction (PAL)
lead: Power-assisted liposuction (PAL) is a surgical body-contouring technique in which a motor drives the cannula so that it vibrates or reciprocates rapidly while the surgeon moves it through subcutaneous fat. It is used to remove localised fat from areas such as the abdomen, flanks, thighs and, in men, the chest, with the aim of a slimmer, more defined silhouette. It is one of several liposuction techniques, alongside tumescent, ultrasound-assisted, laser-assisted and water-jet-assisted methods.[1]

Proponents of the technique say the mechanical motion lets surgeons remove fat with less manual effort, and it has been described in published surgical reports for body contouring, superficial liposuction, gynecomastia in men and fat harvesting for grafting.[1][2][3] In looksmaxxing communities it is mentioned mainly as a body-contouring option within the broader category of liposuction.

Published evidence consists mostly of surgeons' case series and small comparative studies; few randomized trials compare PAL with conventional suction-assisted liposuction, and the procedure is a surgical operation with the same general risk categories as other forms of liposuction.[1][4]
infobox: Local (tumescent), regional or general, depending on extent[1]

paras: In conventional liposuction a surgeon manually pushes and pulls a hollow cannula connected to suction through the fat layer. In power-assisted liposuction the cannula is attached to a handpiece that moves it back and forth at high frequency, a design that its advocates say reduces surgeon fatigue and speeds fat removal.[1] The procedure is usually combined with tumescent infiltration of local anesthetic solution.[1]

Modern liposuction began in the mid-1970s in Rome, where Arpad and Giorgio Fischer developed suction with a blunt cannula, first for the outer thighs. Yves-Gerard Illouz later developed the wet technique, injecting saline and hyaluronidase before suction, and in the 1980s the American dermatologist Jeffrey Klein introduced tumescent anesthesia with dilute lidocaine and epinephrine, which made local anesthesia alone possible.[1]

Power-assisted liposuction followed as one of several newer energy-assisted variants. Wikipedia describes PAL as using a vibrating cannula to remove more fat with less surgeon effort and says it is often used for scarred areas or large fat harvests.[1] In 2015, liposuction surpassed breast augmentation as the most common cosmetic procedure in the US, according to Wikipedia.[1]

Reports describe PAL used with a pull-through approach to treat gynecomastia in men, in which fat and glandular tissue are removed through small incisions.[3] Surgeons have also used powered or vibrating cannulas to harvest fat for transfer, including large-volume gluteal fat grafting.[4][5]

Superficial liposuction, which works in the fat layer close to the skin to improve contour, has its own published complication analysis covering 2,398 cases, although that review concerns superficial technique in general rather than power assistance specifically.[6]

Wikipedia lists common liposuction targets as the thighs, abdomen (including abdominal etching) and hips, and notes use for gynecomastia and lipomas, often combined with other body-contouring procedures. Small-volume procedures (under 1,000 cc) are often done awake, while large-volume procedures (over 5,000 cc) require anesthesia and hospital stays.[1]

Complications described for liposuction in general include pain, bruising, swelling, contour irregularities, altered sensation, infection, bleeding, blood clots and, rarely, death, according to summaries of the literature.[1] A US survey of liposuction practice published in 2011 documented trends in how the procedure is performed and by whom.[7] Risk is reported to rise with the volume removed.[1]

Wikipedia cites a 2015 study of 4,534 patients that found complications in 1.5%, with volumes above 100 ml per BMI unit associated with higher risk, and estimates deaths at about one per 10,000 cases as of 2011. It lists deep vein thrombosis, organ perforation, bleeding, infection and fat embolism among serious risks, and says liposuction does not address obesity-related metabolic problems.[1] The 2011 ASAPS survey (492 respondents, 28.7% response) found suction-assisted lipectomy preferred by 51.4%; ultrasound-assisted, laser-assisted and suction-assisted methods were most often linked to complications, and only 10.5% used laser-assisted liposuction yet 38% had treated a patient with a complication from it.[7]

Gynecomastia series: a 2008 review of 99 consecutive patients (197 breasts) treated between January 2003 and November 2006 used PAL with a pull-through technique to remove fatty breast tissue and then fibroglandular tissue through the liposuction incision. Ninety-six patients (192 breasts) were successfully treated, average aspirate was 459 ml per breast (25 to 1,400 ml), complications occurred in 1.0% of breasts and no revisions were required.[3]

Randomised comparison: a 2007 trial of 60 patients with BMI 25 to 30 compared power water-assisted liposuction (n=32) with traditional liposuction (n=28). Pain differed significantly: at 4 days, 87% of power-assisted patients were pain-free versus 3.6% of the traditional group, and bruising was less in the power-assisted group. The authors concluded that power water-assisted liposuction causes very little pain and less tissue trauma. The device was power water-assisted, not a plain vibrating cannula.[8]

Fat harvesting: a 2014 study split samples from nine abdominoplasty donors between PAL and manual aspiration. Cell count, proliferation and viability did not differ significantly, and PAL-harvested cells showed higher expression of adiponectin, GLUT4 and PPAR-gamma, leading the authors to call PAL a feasible way to harvest viable adipose-derived stem cells.[9] Powered or vibrating cannulas have also been described for large-volume gluteal fat grafting.[4][5]

Registered studies: a 2026 trial (NCT07820397) is comparing adipose tissue viability after different liposuction approaches within the same patients,[10] and a registered study of harmonic vibration liposuction (NCT07889427) enrolled 13 participants.[11] Most other published work is descriptive surgical technique reports.[3][4]

lore.intro: Power-assisted liposuction appears in forum discussions of body-contouring surgery, usually as one named option among liposuction technologies rather than as a looksmaxxing topic in its own right.

claims.claim: A vibrating cannula gives smoother, more precise fat removal than manual liposuction
claims.believers: Proponents, including some surgeons who use the technique, say the motion lets the cannula glide through fat with less force, which they associate with less surgeon fatigue and finer sculpting.[1]
claims.experts: Published comparisons are few; a randomized trial of postoperative pain used a power water-assisted device rather than a plain vibrating cannula, and surgical reports are largely descriptive.[8]

card.summary: A motorized, vibrating-cannula version of liposuction; documented in surgical reports but with little head-to-head trial evidence.
card.note: Surgical procedure; carries general liposuction risks.

quick.overview:
Power-assisted liposuction uses a cannula driven by a motor so it vibrates while moving through fat. It is a variant of ordinary liposuction used for body contouring, male chest reduction and fat harvesting.

Published work is mostly surgeons describing their technique. Few randomized comparisons with conventional liposuction exist.
quick.mechanism: A motorized handpiece moves the suction cannula rapidly back and forth, which proponents say reduces manual effort for the surgeon and eases passage through fat. It is typically paired with tumescent anesthetic solution.
quick.risks: As an operation, it shares liposuction risks reported in the literature, including pain, bruising, contour irregularities, infection, bleeding and clots, with rare deaths; risk is reported to increase with volume removed.

chain: Targeted areas such as abdomen, flanks or male chest lose volume
angle.text: Surgeons use PAL to remove stubborn fat in chosen areas, including male chest fat in gynecomastia, so the contour looks leaner. Wikipedia notes that overall body fat usually returns to pre-treatment levels within months, often in the abdomen, so results depend on weight stability.
